articles.title: US Prepares Historic Visa Revocation for Asylum Seekers
articles.content: xwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoAn Essex County police officer walks past a tent used by protestors as a base outside of Delaney Hall, in Newark, New Jersey, US, May 31, 2026 [File: David 'Dee' Delgado/ Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and AP25 Aug 2026The United States is preparing to cancel business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the country, according to the Associated Press news agency. The AP, citing State Department documents and interviews with two US officials, reported on Monday that if the plan goes ahead, it would be the “largest single mass revocation of visas” in the country’s history. It said the State Department is expected to announce the action within the coming weeks, working in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). It would target so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026, whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum. “We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” said State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott. Officials cited by the AP said the revocations would not automatically trigger deportations. Instead, most people with pending asylum cases would be shifted into a different immigration category, effectively stripping their business or tourist designation while their cases proceed. In a social media post on Monday, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau called out people who he said try to use tourist and business visas to get into the US and then apply for asylum. “People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims,” Landau wrote on X. “Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law.” Since President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants – demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds for the processing of visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries. In the past 18 months, the State Department has also revoked about 175,000 visas for people who have been convicted or accused of crimes ranging from drunk driving to rape and robbery, as well as for people who have spoken out publicly against US policies, particularly in the Middle East.

The administration views this as a measure to deter what it labels 'asylum fraud' and enforce stricter border controls.

Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP View image in fullscreen Anthony Albanese will tell national cabinet his government will legislate next year to ensure the benefits of AI and datacentres are shared among states. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP Albanese seeks to quell datacentre disquiet as climate expert warns ‘we’ve got one shot to get the rules right’ Prime minister will use national cabinet meeting to assuage premiers over new AI law as Aemo forecasts seven-fold rise in datacentre power use Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Anthony Albanese will seek to use Wednesday’s high-stakes talks with premiers to quell growing unhappiness about national controls on datacentre developments , promising new approval laws will complement state rules. Faced with growing opposition from conservative governments in Queensland and the Northern Territory, Albanese will tell national cabinet he plans a major piece of legislation next year to ensure the economic benefits of AI are shared widely. With potential to be one of the major reforms of Labor’s second term, the new law will set tough copyright rules for AI businesses and impose standards for security, safety and skills development. The meeting on Wednesday will come after the latest forecast from the Australian Energy Market Operator showing datacentre power use is projected to increase seven-fold over the next decade. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The industry’s rapid growth, driven by increasing reliance on AI and cloud computing, remained one of the most significant causes of growth in electricity demand, according to Aemo’s annual Electricity Statement of Opportunities. In addition to 165 datacentres already operating around the country, a further 225 are in development, the report showed, reflecting a substantial increase in new proposals compared to 2025, Aemo said on Tuesday. Datacentre electricity demand was expected to grow from 5 to 34 terawatt hours by 2035-36, the report said, growing from 3% of overall consumption to 13%. AEMO said high datacentre growth could see consumption reach 52 TWh – a 10-fold increase over the decade. But there were high levels of uncertainty, with more than a third of projects listed in 2025 since cancelled, and operating facilities taking years to ramp to full capacity. Daniel Westerman, Aemo’s chief executive, said record levels of new generation and storage coming online had improved the outlook for reliability, even with the expected retirement of coal power stations. “The reliability outlook has improved, supported by record levels of new generation and storage, and a strong pipeline of projects expected over the next decade.” Report supporting Australia’s teen social media ban appears to contain AI hallucinations, Senate hears Read more The Climate Council chief executive, Amanda McKenzie, said datacentres were set “to devour an enormous share of Australia’s electricity in the coming years”. “We’ve got one shot to get the rules right now and ensure that datacentre growth doesn’t strain our grid and push up pollution.” Albanese will use national cabinet to strike agreement on a plan to legislate nationally consistent minimum obligations for datacentres, requiring them not to push up energy prices, meet their own infrastructure costs and minimise water use. The rules will also require developers to minimise the effect of new datacentres on local communities, ensuring they are appropriately sized and appropriately located, away from homes, schools and potential housing or agricultural sites. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion Projects approved for development before the new rules come into place will only be subject to existing state and territory laws. Last month, the prime minister promised “the strongest possible protection” for Australian creatives against misuse of their work by artificial intelligence models. He said it would be “theft” if writers, artists and musicians didn’t have control of their work or receive payment for its use in training large AI models. Combining the elements into a single piece of legislation signals the government’s ambition on AI, but could also heighten the political risk of getting the bill through parliament ahead of the next election. Queensland premier David Crisafulli and the NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, have signalled opposition to federal rules requiring datacentres to be powered by renewable projects at the exclusion of coal and gas. Albanese is expected to seek broad consensus, but could be challenged by the increasingly outspoken Liberal-National and Country Liberal party leaders. He will also discuss state opposition to the national gun buy-back, which only has support from New South Wales and the ACT so far. Action to curb violence against women and the growing H1 bird flu crisis are also on the agenda. Anger about Western Australia’s favourable GST share will also flare. articles.title: Goldman Sachs Warns Against AI Eroding Banker Skills
articles.content: LivestreamMenuAI could erode bankers’ reasoning skills if employees rely on models to do their analytical work, warns Chris Churchman, who leads Marquee, Goldman's digital platform for institutional clients.Banks need to find a balance between using AI and preserving Wall Street's apprenticeship culture, Churchman said in an interview on the firm's "Exchanges" podcast. Goldman is still figuring out how to balance AI with human involvement, said Churchman. One of the biggest challenges with generative AI is around accuracy, he said. In this article A Goldman Sachs partner leading one of the bank's flagship artificial intelligence projects warned that AI's spread across Wall Street risks hobbling the thinking capabilities of the next generation of financiers. "There's a huge danger here that in the era of AI, we outsource our reasoning to these models, and we have cognitive atrophy that stops us being able to reason from first principles ourselves," said Chris Churchman, who leads Goldman's digital platform for institutional clients called Marquee. The comments came during the latest episode of the firm's "Exchanges" podcast, according to a transcript provided exclusively to CNBC. Just as people lost navigation and memorization skills with modern inventions, bankers risk losing analytical abilities if algorithms handle all the heavy lifting, Churchman said. "Reasoning is still important," he said. "You still need to reason about [problems] and structure it into an argument, and now we're delegating reasoning." Wall Street's push to enmesh AI into all of its trading and banking processes could be a kind of devil's bargain: It will make the industry more profitable today while potentially eroding the talent it needs for tomorrow. With AI taking over more of the routine work that has traditionally taught young bankers and traders how to think and make decisions, firms risk sacrificing the culture that turns junior employees into seasoned Wall Street talent. It could even reduce the need for junior bankers in the first place. Last year, CNBC reported that Wall Street firms were examining ways of using AI to lower the ratio of junior bankers to senior employees. Banks need to find a balance between using AI and preserving Wall Street's apprenticeship culture, said Churchman, who ran currency trading at UBS before joining Goldman in 2021. "You learn by doing, and a lot of knowledge is tacit, it was never written down," he said. Goldman needs "to make sure we don't lose that tacit and intuitive knowledge that some of our best people have today [and] to ensure the next generation have it too," Churchman said. For instance, junior traders learn by fielding client pricing requests under supervision of experienced risk takers, Churchman said. "We can absolutely automate that," he said, "but then do we get the senior traders that fully understand?" Systems must be designed so that employees still call the shots in high-stakes, high-uncertainty decisions rather than becoming passive operators, Churchman said. Even Goldman, one of the world's top investment banks, hasn't yet "figured out" how it will manage the transition the company has begun, said Churchman, who is also co-chair of the firm's Global Banking and Markets AI working group. Also in the podcast interview, Churchman shared lessons from implementing AI into Marquee, which is used by hedge funds and other institutional clients to access Goldman's market data, research, risk analytics and trade execution services. The Marquee AI platform is only available to Goldman employees for now, he said. The toughest challenge, from a technical standpoint, is in ensuring that AI answers are 100% factual and can be audited, he said. While consumer AI chatbots warn users of possible mistakes, in high finance, the tolerance for errors is low. Churchman said that in developing the firm's AI platform for clients, the software made a startling admission. "When we challenged it hard, at least it was honest," Churchman said. "It was like, 'Look, in the end, I'm better at sounding thorough than being thorough.'"

articles.title: China Delays Moon Mission, Fueling Speculation
articles.content: China’s manned space agency said on Sunday it is delaying a research moon mission that is part of Beijing’s efforts to land a crew there by 2030, less than two weeks after a rare launch failure. The Chang’e-7 lunar probe on a Long March 5 carrier rocket. Photo: CCTV screenshot. The agency said after a “comprehensive assessment” the mission, which involved sending the Chang’e-7 lunar probe on a Long March 5 carrier rocket, “does not meet launch conditions and cannot take place during the planned window this year”. The decision to delay was “based on the principle of prudence, reliability and absolute mission success,” it added, without providing further details on what conditions weren’t met or when the launch would be rescheduled. The mission — meant to search for water on the moon’s south pole — was scheduled to depart either over the weekend or Monday, according to media reports. Last week, the agency said the probe and carrier rocket had been moved to the takeoff area at Wenchang Space Launch Center in southern Hainan province. As of Wednesday, the takeoff site and equipment were in good condition, with inspections to take place and a launch “scheduled for the coming period”. The Chang’e-7 delay comes just under two weeks after media reports showed a rocket launched from the Hainan site had exploded, as crowds watched a fiery ball in the sky. The failed mission involved a Long March 7A carrier rocket, which had lifted off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site, state news agency Xinhua said at the time. China’s Long March 7A carrier rocket exploded on Monday, August 10, 2026. Photo: Supplied. An “anomaly” occurred when the rocket carrying the Zhongxing-4B communications satellite was in flight, Xinhua added. The cause of the failure was under investigation, it said. Beijing has ploughed billions of dollars into its space programme in recent years to achieve what President Xi Jinping calls the country’s “space dream”. China successfully landed a reusable rocket for the first time in July, according to its space agency, marking a major step in its space ambitions and in reducing launch costs. The country is aiming to land astronauts on the Moon before 2030, a race in which the United States is also competing with its Artemis programme. articles.title: Japanese Lawmakers Propose AI Copyright Safeguards
articles.content: Japan’s Cabinet Office has proposed a revised Principle-Code for generative artificial intelligence (AI) businesses that sets out principles on intellectual property (IP) protection, including avoiding crawling so-called pirate sites, respecting access restrictions such as paywalls, and increasing transparency around how businesses manage IP risks. The draft would use a ‘comply or explain’ approach, under which Generative AI businesses would either follow the principles or explain publicly why they do not. The proposal could give rights holders more information about the models, training data and data-collection methods used by generative AI businesses, while leaving Japan’s existing copyright framework largely intact. It also puts transparency around data collection into a non-binding governance framework that would cover Japanese businesses and foreign businesses whose Generative AI systems or services are available in Japan. The revised “Principle-Code for Protection of Intellectual Property and Transparency for the Appropriate Use of Generative AI” was discussed by the Study Group on Intellectual Property Rights in the AI Era on August 18 . The Cabinet Office’s meeting materials identify it as a revised draft, with changes made after a public consultation that ran from December 26, 2025 to January 26, 2026. The proposed code would apply to generative AI developers and providers, including businesses outside Japan whose generative AI systems or services are provided in Japan or made available to Japanese nationals. It is intended to balance the development of generative AI with the protection of intellectual property rights and greater transparency for rights holders and users. Protecting copyrighted works during AI development The draft says generative AI businesses should establish principles for protecting IP rights and clarify responsibility for implementing them. It also proposes that businesses review these principles at least once a year and publish their substance. The draft says businesses should establish processes to ensure that their use of data to develop and train generative AI does not infringe others’ intellectual property rights. It calls on them to respect access restrictions, including paywalls, and to use crawlers that follow machine-readable instructions such as robots.txt. It also asks them to endeavour to avoid crawling so-called pirate sites, to disclose their crawler measures for each user agent, and to give notice when those measures change. That puts the acquisition and use of training data within the proposed governance framework. The principles therefore address how businesses obtain training material, not only what their models generate. Training and output safeguards The draft also proposes that businesses retain training-related logs for a certain period. Where possible, it asks them to take technical measures to prevent infringing outputs. As far as possible, it asks them to use measures such as digital watermarking and C2PA to verify content origin and provenance. Businesses would also be expected to establish contact points for rights holders, make the requirements for an approach as clear as possible, and keep records of their responses. They would also be expected to tell users of their AI not to use outputs that appear to infringe. More transparency around training data The proposed framework also sets out ways for rights holders to seek information about the use of their works in AI development. The draft does not require businesses to release every individual item of training data publicly. It does, however, contemplate public disclosure of specified information about models, training data and collection methods, alongside a mechanism for a rights holder pursuing a legal remedy to ask whether a specific URL or identifier they name was used in training or validation, limited to what the business can readily access and confirm. AI users would have an equivalent mechanism in relation to their own outputs. It also recognises limits where the information is proprietary, including trade secrets. Japan has also examined this issue through its broader IP policy . Its intellectual property strategy materials identify transparency around training data and the relationship between AI development and copyrighted works as areas requiring further attention. The proposal comes as the legal treatment of AI training remains under active discussion internationally. MediaNama has previously reported on the copyright questions surrounding generative AI training, including when using copyrighted material to train a model can amount to infringement. Japan is particularly relevant to that debate because Article 30-4 of its Copyright Act permits certain uses of copyrighted works for purposes such as data analysis, including AI training, subject to specified conditions. A March 2024 document adopted by a subcommittee of the Council for Cultural Affairs said Article 30-4 can permit the use of copyrighted works for AI development and other data-analysis purposes without permission from the copyright holder where the statutory conditions are met. That document also said the exception does not apply where there is a purpose of enjoying the work, that it can fail where material is taken by circumventing access restrictions or from a paid database, and that businesses should strictly refrain from deliberately collecting from known pirate sites – the same ground the draft code now covers. Japan is proposing governance around that copyright framework The draft code does not amend Japan’s existing copyright rules. Instead, it proposes governance and disclosure practices for training data, IP protection and related safeguards. That distinction is visible in the proposed “comply or explain” model. The framework is presented as a non-binding code rather than a new statutory obligation backed by a penalty. Japan also has a broader AI governance framework under the Act on Promotion of Research and Development, and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-related Technology. The law was promulgated on June 4, 2025, and came fully into force on September 1, 2025. The government adopted an AI Basic Plan under that framework by Cabinet decision on December 23, 2025. The IP principle code sits within that wider AI policy effort rather than amending the Copyright Act. The code is still a draft The August 18 document is not a law or regulation. Examples include respecting access restrictions, avoiding pirate sites, retaining training-related logs, creating channels for rights holders and using measures such as watermarking and C2PA. articles.title: Google's AI-First 'Googlebook' Laptop Faces Copilot+ Challenge
articles.content: Written by Steven Vaughan-Nichols, Senior Contributing Editor Senior Contributing Editor Aug. 24, 2026 at 5:48 a.m. PT Google / ZDNET Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google. ZDNET's key takeaways The Googlebook is more about AI than Android compatibility. The new operating system will merge Android and ChromeOS. Chromebooks will continue to be sold and supported. One of the best computers I ever used was Google's 2015 Chromebook Pixel . In fact, 11 years later, I'm still using it. I'm also still annoyed that Google never released another publicly available model . Recently, Google began its reentry into the laptop market with the Googlebook, with help from HP, Acer, Lenovo, Dell, and Asus . Also:  First look at Googlebook: A premium Chromebook alternative for Android users This release, however, won't be a high-end Chromebook like the Pixel. Instead, it's the latest manifestation of Google's plan to converge Android and ChromeOS . This scheme has been in the works -- I kid you not -- since 2009. We now think (fingers crossed) that the Googlebook will make their pairing work sometime in September. This new premium laptop category will combine Android's application ecosystem with ChromeOS's browser strengths and put Gemini AI at the machine's heart . If this sounds to you like Microsoft's Copilot+ PCs , you're right -- it does. Google can only hope it will sell better than Microsoft's AI-first laptops have so far . Googlebook plans Google calls Googlebook "the next generation of ChromeOS," built with parts of the Android stack to give applications "laptop-class" behavior and native-level performance. This new combo operating system is known as Aluminum OS . Reportedly, this Linux-based operating system will combine ChromeOS and Android. What we don't have, though, is much in the way of details about how Aluminum will work . The key public promise is that Googlebook with Aluminum will combine Android apps and Chrome with Android phone integration. Googlebook users will be able to work across phones and laptops without manually shifting gears between phones, tablets, and laptops. For example, Quick Access should enable you to browse, search, and insert files stored on a phone directly from the laptop file browser, without transfers. This, or so fans insist, will make this new technology competitive with Apple's Mac, iPhone, and iPad family. Also:  Chromebook vs. Googlebook: How I'm deciding which laptop to upgrade to next We also still don't know what the Googlebook's processors, memory configurations, storage tiers, or prices will look like. There have been leaks from Googlebook original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) such as HP , Acer , and Lenovo , but the nuts and bolts are still a mystery. Put all the leaks together, and it looks like Googlebook will launch as a premium, multi-form-factor laptop line. These won't replace the low-cost Chromebook tier we all know. The strongest claimed configuration is Acer's 14-inch OLED system at roughly $1,200, while Lenovo's detachable Duet M points to a 13-inch MediaTek-powered option. Asus and HP leaks chiefly reveal design and continuity software rather than core specifications. All remain unconfirmed pending Google and OEM announcements. Google Gemini becomes the interface The company's most consequential design decision may be to treat Gemini not as an optional chatbot but as a system-level interaction layer. Its flagship example is Magic Pointer. This feature activates when you "wiggle" the cursor and offers contextual Gemini suggestions based on the content under the pointer. Google says this could include turning a date in an email into a calendar event or combining selected images to visualize a piece of furniture in a room. Also:  Googlebook looks promising, but one big laptop brand is conspicuously absent A second feature, Create Your Widget, will let people generate custom desktop widgets through prompts. Google says Gemini can search the web or connect to Google services such as Gmail and Calendar to assemble a personalized desktop dashboard -- for instance, displaying travel information, reservations, and a countdown for an upcoming trip. Those features. make Googlebook a test of whether a vendor can turn generative AI from an application into an operating-system-level convenience without adding complexity, privacy concerns, or unwanted automation. Google has not yet detailed the local-versus-cloud processing model for these Gemini functions, the data-retention policy for screen context, or which capabilities will require paid AI subscriptions. Android app compatibility Google's developer materials point to an Android-first application strategy rather than simply continuing the Chromebook model of running Android apps alongside web software. Existing Android applications will run on Googlebook, Google says, while developers are being encouraged to adapt them for keyboard, mouse, trackpad, stylus, and game-controller input; file handling and printing; custom cursors; drag-and-drop; resizable windows; and multiple simultaneous app instances. Also:  Google's AI can see your business data by default in Workspace - unless you disable it That development push matters because Android's historical advantage -- its large mobile app catalog -- does not automatically translate into high-quality laptop software. Googlebook's credibility will hinge on whether familiar Android titles can feel native in long-form, multiwindow desktop work rather than merely functional on a large display. Where Aluminum OS fits "Aluminum OS" is widely reported as the internal name for the platform unifying Android and ChromeOS, but Google hasn't used it in its announcements. Google's public language instead refers to Googlebook as the "next generation of ChromeOS" and says it is built with parts of the Android stack. Also:  This free Android assistant fixes my biggest Gemini frustration - and keeps my data private That distinction is important. Googlebook is the market-facing laptop category; Aluminum OS appears to be the project or codename associated with the Android-and-ChromeOS convergence underneath it. Reporting on the codename has described it as an Android-based desktop platform, but Google has yet to provide a full architectural account of what remains from ChromeOS, whether the ChromeOS brand will persist, or whether and how existing Chromebooks could migrate. Looking ahead Personally, I'm sure both Chromebooks and Googlebooks will continue. It makes sense. Chromebooks are great for students and people like me, who need an inexpensive laptop for web-based work that can also double as a Linux laptop. Googlebooks will be for people who are willing to pay real money for an AI-first laptop. Also:  5 ways I speed up my Android phone beyond clearing system cache - all for free For now, Googlebook represents a strategic attempt to give AI a serious laptop form factor. The unanswered questions -- Android interoperability, device pricing, offline and Linux capabilities, enterprise management, update policy, ChromeOS migration, app quality, and the boundaries of Gemini's access to user data -- will determine whether Google has created a true Chromebook successor or simply a more AI-forward, Android-oriented laptop. articles.title: DOT Mandates Biometric SIM Checks in India
articles.content: You can access the notification here . The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) notified the Telecommunications (User Identification) Rules, 2026 on August 21, making biometric identification mandatory before a person can get, change, or disconnect a mobile SIM. The rules took effect on the day they were published and follow the draft rules DoT released for consultation in September 2025. Which services does this cover? DoT notified two services under Section 3(7) of the Act: Wireless access services , which covers mobile SIM connections. Internet telephony service through mobile user terminals , which covers app-based calling over mobile. The second entry brings internet telephony under biometric user identification. DoT has not clarified whether this covers over-the-top (OTT) calling apps. This follows DoT’s separate SIM-binding directive to WhatsApp and Telegram under the Telecommunication Cybersecurity Amendment Rules, 2025, which MediaNama has tracked through RTIs and a stakeholder discussion . When must an operator run biometric identification? An authorised entity, which is the telecom operator, must run biometric identification at four points: Before enrolling a user for a new SIM. Before updating a user’s information. Before disconnecting a connection. When DoT directs re-verification. What are the two verification routes? The rules set two methods, and which one applies depends on whether the user holds Aadhaar: e-KYC , for an Aadhaar number holder. The operator authenticates the user’s information through the Aadhaar e-KYC authentication facility and stores the e-KYC data, including the Aadhaar number, received from the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI). D-KYC , for a user who does not hold Aadhaar, or who holds Aadhaar but cannot complete face, fingerprint, or iris capture because of an impairment, disfigurement, injury, or amputation. The operator conducts a live capture of the user’s face, captures images of identity and address documents, and verifies that the live face matches both the user and the photograph on the document. What can the operator do to verify a user? Under the D-KYC route, the operator can verify a user’s identity or address claim through a field visit, seek police assistance, or do both. If a user cannot undergo live face capture, the operator must offer an accessible alternative using other biometric information. What happens with impersonation or forged documents? If an operator finds that false, incorrect, or forged information or documents were used, or that a user impersonated another person, it must: Inform the police or the relevant law enforcement agency to register a first information report (FIR). Report the steps taken to DoT through the portal. If the operator fails to act, DoT can direct it to file the FIR and can initiate action against the operator under Chapter VIII of the Act. How does the confirmation alert work? DoT can require an operator to send an alert to a user’s existing connections, asking the user to confirm that they made the request. If the user responds that they did not, the operator must act immediately until it establishes the facts. It must suspend a new connection, reverse or hold an information change, or reverse or hold a disconnection, depending on which request triggered the alert. What are the user’s obligations? The operator must clearly explain to each user that they have to: Provide correct information to establish their identity. Not provide false, forged, or incorrect documents, suppress material information, or impersonate anyone, as prohibited under Section 29(a) of the Act. Not resell, transfer, or lease their SIM to another user, except for transfers to relatives or legal heirs under the rules. A user who furnishes false particulars or impersonates another person faces action under Section 33 and Section 42(3)(e) of the Act. The restriction on transfers to relatives and legal heirs carries over from the draft. MediaNama flagged at the draft stage that this ignores how families informally share a single SIM. What about business connections? For a business connection, the operator verifies the authorised representative of the business and every end user on the connection. If an end user changes, the representative must inform the operator and get the new end user biometrically identified within the period specified on the portal. If they fail to do so, the operator must suspend the connection. DoT can exempt an end user or a class of end users from biometric identification, with reasons recorded in writing. How long do operators have to comply? Operators have three months from the date the rules came into force to build the technical, organisational, and infrastructure measures required for compliance. DoT can extend this period by up to three more months if it finds that operators are not ready, in the public interest. Questions this raises Does biometric identification now apply to WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram calling? DoT has not defined “internet telephony through mobile user terminals”. If it covers OTT apps, it would add to the existing SIM-binding directive to WhatsApp and Telegram. Does this duplicate Aadhaar KYC without Aadhaar’s safeguards? The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) asked at the draft stage why a parallel biometric system is needed and whether it carries the same consent, retention, and correction safeguards as the Aadhaar framework. How long is biometric and document data retained, and how is it secured? The rules say that the subscriber data record must follow applicable data-protection law, without specifying a retention period, a deletion rule, or an encryption standard. How this sits with the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act remains unclear. Does the fraud premise hold? MediaNama Founder-Editor Nikhil Pahwa has asked why extending the same telecom identifier to a new ecosystem would increase trust, when years of Aadhaar-based ASTR verification have not reduced fraud. What happens to informal SIM-sharing? The transfer restriction to relatives and legal heirs blocks the ordinary practice of one family member buying a SIM that others use, a concern MediaNama raised at the draft stage. articles.title: ChatGPT Work Offers Agentic AI Tips, Raises Productivity Questions
articles.content: Written by David Gewirtz, Senior Contributing Editor Senior Contributing Editor Aug. 24, 2026 at 4:59 a.m. PT Elyse Betters Picaro / ZDNET Follow ZDNET:  Add us as a preferred source  on Google. ZDNET's key takeaways ChatGPT Work can browse, manage files, and complete tasks. Free users can try it, but paid plans offer more capacity. Start small, limit permissions, and double-check its work. ChatGPT answers questions. ChatGPT Work does work. That's because ChatGPT Work is agentic , which is a fancy way of describing how some AIs can go off and accomplish a series of tasks. Because ChatGPT has become more capable, the differences between ChatGPT and ChatGPT Work can be subtle. For example, if you ask ChatGPT to plan a travel itinerary, it will search the web and gather together a list of great destinations. That's the AI doing something. Also: 'I can't stop': 80% of developers find AI coding more addictive than helpful It gets even more blurry with ChatGPT's Deep Research mode . Deep Research is essentially a special-purpose agentic web researcher. Deep Research can dig around the web and build a much deeper analysis than ChatGPT. ChatGPT Work can do all that, and more. It can open your own Web browser, or its own internal one. It can move around the web on screen (rather than or in addition to retrieving a web page's HTML data). It can create and move files. It can process through a long sequence of steps. This approach is very much like what an AI agentic programming tool like Claude Code or OpenAI's Codex  can do. In fact, agentic work tools like Claude Cowork and ChatGPT Work evolved directly out of agentic coding tools that some users decided to use for non-coding tasks. Also:  This AI expert says the job apocalypse isn't coming, even if you're a coder - here's why Following a surprising usage surge in non-programmer use of those programmer tools, both Anthropic with Claude and OpenAI with ChatGPT launched agentic work products. Today, we'll investigate starting with ChatGPT Work. What you need for ChatGPT Work ChatGPT Work is available for all ChatGPT users, even those on the free tier . There are limits, though. Agentic operations take a lot of AI juice (typically measured in tokens). Free users are given access to only a small amount of capacity. As you pay more, you get more usage capacity. I have been using the $20/mo ChatGPT Plus , which has proven to be pretty capable. When I use Codex for coding, it tends to slam shut after about five hours of intense work. Still, that's five hours of intense work for $20. That usage limit resets after a while. I've found I can get about 20 or so hours of agentic coding done each month on that tier. ChatGPT Work uses a similar amount of capacity. You can probably do a fairly large project with Work every few days and not feel all that limited on the $20/mo plan. Unfortunately, OpenAI (and this is true of all the AI companies) doesn't have a single metric that you can measure by. Each request requires a different mix of resources, so an absolute usage capacity isn't really possible. But I'd think of it this way: free gets you a taste, $20/mo gets you fairly regular moderate usage, and the higher tiers let you binge. Also:  75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code - here's why they choose it over Codex Beyond your account, you'll need to either sign in to the ChatGPT web page or download the desktop app . For any tasks you want to run on your computer, you'll need the desktop app. Note that up until mid-July, the ChatGPT desktop app was a chat app. Then, in July, OpenAI combined ChatGPT, Work, and Codex into a "super app," which had the unfortunate side-effect of killing some of the ChatGPT app's best features . So now, if you want to use ChatGPT Work on the desktop, download the ChatGPT desktop app.  Also:  I loved ChatGPT Desktop until OpenAI gutted it to make room for Codex and Work You can ignore my grumbling about the removed features. OpenAI still hasn't bothered to put them back in. But I'm not bitter. It's been almost two months. I'm not holding a grudge. Not at all. How to use ChatGPT Work Once you launch ChatGPT using either the desktop app or in your browser, you'll see two buttons above the chat message bar. One is Chat, and one is Work. The interface changes when you switch between Chat and Work modes. Screenshot by David Gewirtz/ZDNET Clicking the buttons (above) changes the mode. On the top, we're in Chat mode. On the bottom, we're in Work mode. Notice also the option to choose the folder you're working in on the bottom. This approach means you can restrict a complex work project to a single folder or hierarchy. Also:  A low-tech solution from the past may be your best defense against AI deepfakes Now, all you do is prompt the AI just like you always have. The difference is that Work can do a lot more. Last month, for example, I had ChatGPT Work dig through a large collection of PDF files, rename them, and organize them in topics. You can read about how I approached this project here . One thing that did make me nervous is that Work hasn't been asking for permissions as often as I'd like. I've generally learned to tune my requests so it doesn't have a reason to run amok, but I would prefer to be asked for an okay more often. An example research project Before I set you loose on ChatGPT Work, I'd like to show you a research project I gave the tool. I'm planning an article comparing vertical mice, and I want to test a bunch of them to see which works best. But I don't just want vertical mice. I want wireless vertical mice that can switch between two to three devices (three preferred). I started digging through Amazon and realized I'd spend an hour or more trawling specs because the product headline doesn't always indicate how many devices a mouse supports. Also:  You can earn your Google Al Professional Certificate for free - and I highly recommend it Then I remembered that I have an agentic AI at my disposal. It was time to delegate. I gave ChatGPT Work one prompt that consisted of the following components: I want you to do some Amazon research for me. I want you to find wireless vertical mice. That was my basic overview. You're going to research mice on Amazon. Then I discussed the key restriction that would narrow the search and save me time: They must be able to switch between at least two Bluetooth wireless devices (but I prefer three). Ignore vertical mice that aren't wireless and ignore vertical mice that only support one computer. Finally, I gave it an assignment only ChatGPT Work (and not ChatGPT or ChatGPT Deep Research) could do. I told it to check each candidate for Prime shipping and fairly immediate availability, and then open each one in its own tab. I wanted to quickly toggle between tabs, close ones I was uninterested in, and then narrow my evaluation scope: When you find them, open each candidate in its own tab. Only choose mice that are Prime and will ship in less than a week. As you can see in the image below, that process took ChatGPT a little over 10 minutes, during which I went and got myself a nice cup of coffee and played with the dog: I used Work to research Amazon products. Screenshot by David Gewirtz/ZDNET Ten quick tips Here are some tips I recommend, based on my experience: When possible, feed the AI small assignments one at a time. For longer projects, ask the AI for a plan before it executes anything. Check your usage availability in Settings > Usage. If you're about to give the AI a big project and your usage availability is low, it will stop mid-run. That sucks. Don't give the AI any passwords. Ever. If you're going to have the AI do anything destructive (like reorganize a folder), make very sure you have a backup or five. And make sure the backups are well out of the AI's reach. Don't believe anything the AI tells you. Double-check everything. Don't be upset if the AI is stupid. Expect it to be. The AI can also be very helpful, but you have to pace and lead it with care and attention. If you're about to start a long, tedious task, ask yourself if the AI can step in instead. Delegation is a good skill. If you decide to use the Gmail connector to send email messages, have the AI create drafts. Review each draft before pressing send. When you set up a connection, you need to grant permissions. Give the fewest permissions you can. It's fairly safe to allow reads. But anything that involves writing, deleting, sending, or otherwise taking an action can backfire. Well, there you go. I've found that I'm using ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork more and more. I switch between the two mostly so I can share my experiences with you. Frankly, my experience has been that both are pretty much on par. And with that, let's call it a day. Have you used an agentic AI coworker like ChatGPT Work? Let us know in the comments below. You can follow my day-to-day project updates on social media. Be sure to subscribe to my weekly update newsletter , and follow me on Twitter/X at @DavidGewirtz , on Facebook at Facebook.com/DavidGewirtz , on Instagram at Instagram.com/DavidGewirtz , on Bluesky at @DavidGewirtz.com , and on YouTube at YouTube.com/DavidGewirtzTV . articles.title: Smartwatches Face Obsolescence Amid Tech Evolution
articles.content: End of life for tech devices is kind of a fuzzy line. While people on tight budgets, or those who don’t need the latest and greatest features, often use their smartphones, tablets, and watches until they no longer run, the companies behind those devices eventually stop supporting them, which can open the door for hackers. The wording varies by company, and it’s not always set in stone, but at some point, users will stop receiving new features, operating system updates, bug fixes and, most critically, security updates. And for wearers of eight different smartwatches, the next few months will bring an end to at least some of those updates. Apple, Samsung, and Google are all ending or scaling back support for various smartwatch models in the coming months. Some will see updates cease in the coming weeks, while others will continue through year’s end. Regardless of how you’re affected, it might be time to rethink your device. The end of support is generally not because of an issue with the hardware. It has more to do with manufacturer timelines and chipsets. “Smartwatches are deemed end-of-life on a fixed schedule, not because the hardware fails, but because manufacturers preset a support window at launch and stop patching once it expires,” said Judson Dressler, head of the risk operations center at cyber risk company Resilience. “Most of the time it stems from engineering costs associated with maintaining older models and incentivizing new purchases. . . . The watch should maintain most of its functionality after that date. What it stops doing is receiving fixes for newly discovered vulnerabilities.” Here are the watches nearing the end of their lives, at least as far as updates go. Apple designates its products as “ vintage ” between five and seven years after they are last distributed for sale. As of today, that includes all Apple Watch releases through the Series 5. The upcoming release of watchOS 27, however, will move several additional watches to unsupported status. Apple’s list of compatible devices for the new operating system excludes the Apple Watch Series 6, Series 7, Series 8, Apple Watch SE 2nd generation, and the first-gen Apple Watch Ultra. Since the Series 8 and Ultra are still within the window in which Apple generally offers support, this appears to be a hardware compatibility issue. Apple will likely release watchOS 27 sometime in September, though it has not given a firm date yet. Owners of the Galaxy Watch 5 and Watch 5 Pro, both of which came out in 2022, will see some changes to the updates they receive, but it won’t be a complete end of support. Any Wear OS updates issued after the end of this year will not be compatible with those models. However, security updates will continue for the foreseeable future, likely for at least another year. The Google Pixel Watch 2, which hit the market in October 2023, will no longer be guaranteed software updates after October of this year, according to Google’s support page for the watch. That includes both security updates and feature drops. It’s worth noting that Pixel smartphones receive seven years of support, compared with the relatively short window for the watch. If you’ve got one of these smartwatches and don’t have the budget or inclination to upgrade, you’ll want to change some of the ways you use it to guard against putting your data at risk. You should stop using the smartwatch for anything that involves sensitive data, including contactless payments, health metrics, and account logins. Those are the things a hacker would target first, Dressler says. You might also want to be careful about connecting to work or home Wi-Fi networks, as your outdated smartwatch could put them at risk. “The bigger risk for anyone else on the network is that the watch stays paired to a phone and often auto-connects to home or office Wi-Fi,” Dressler says. “An unpatched watch on that network is an unmonitored device most endpoint security tools never scan, and it can serve as a foothold to reach other devices once it’s compromised.” The early-rate deadline for the Most Innovative Companies Awards is Friday, September 4, at 11:59 p.m. PT. articles.title: Amazon Hikes Echo, Kindle, Fire TV Prices Up to 60%
articles.content: Written by Lance Whitney, Contributor Contributor Aug. 24, 2026 at 7:45 a.m. PT Amazon Echo Dot (left), Google Home Speaker (center), Apple HomePod mini (right). Maria Diaz/ZDNET  Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google. ZDNET's key takeaways Amazon has raised prices on Echos, Kindles, and other products. The price of an Echo Dot has risen by 60% to $79.99. Amazon blamed the hikes on the costs of memory and storage chips. Shopping for a new Echo, Kindle, or other Amazon product? You may have to shell out more for the item than you would have less than a week ago. Late last week, Amazon raised prices on several of its key products, according to a  review by  Fortune . The increases affect a few categories, specifically Echos, Kindles, Fire TV sticks, and Amazon eero routers. Looking at the sheer percentages, the price jumps vary. But with the 5th-generation Echo Dot, for example, you'll now pay 60% more to snag one. How much will these devices cost now? Here's a breakdown of all the affected products with the old and new prices, courtesy of our friends at The Verge (subscription required) . Product Old price New price Percentage difference Echo Dot (5th gen) $49.99 $79.99 60% Echo Dot Max $99.99 $119.99 20% Echo Spot $79.99 $109.99 37.50% Echo Show 8 $179.99 $199.99 11.10% Echo Show 11 $219.99 $249.99 13.60% Echo Show 15 $299.99 $349.99 16.70% Echo Show 21 $399.99 $499.99 25% Kindle (16GB) $109.99 $149.99 36.40% Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) $159.99 $199.99 25% Fire TV Stick HD $34.99 $39.99 14.30% Fire TV Stick 4K Max $59.99 $84.99 41.70% eero 7 (3-pack) $349.99 $399.99 14.30% eero Pro 7 (3-pack) $699.99 $799.99 14.30% Why such dramatic price hikes on these core products? It's now become a familiar refrain. Blame the increased costs of memory and storage chips. Also:  Why Amazon's Echo Hub became my favorite way to control my smart home "The consumer electronics industry is facing significant increases in memory and storage component costs," Kristy Schmidt, senior communications manager of Amazon's Devices & Services division, said in a statement shared with ZDNET. "After absorbing these increases for as long as we could, we recently adjusted pricing across our product lines. Our approach has always been to offer great products at accessible prices, and that commitment hasn't changed." AI companies have been grabbing much of the available stock of DRAM and NAND flash storage for their systems and data centers. That move has triggered a severe  chip shortage for everyone else , resulting in price increases on the available supplies. Plus, the major memory manufacturers have shifted their limited resources and budgets toward higher-margin, enterprise components, leaving scraps for the consumer market. In June, Apple upped the prices on certain iPad and MacBook models . A basic iPad with 128GB of storage now starts at $449, up from $349. An iPad Air with 128GB of storage now starts at $749, up from $599. A MacBook Air with ⁠512GB of storage now starts at $1,299, up from $1,099. Also:  Apple's smart home springs a leak - here's everything we expect to see in September At the beginning of August, Microsoft bumped up the prices of its Xbox consoles by $100 for the 512GB models and $150 for the 1TB models. Pinning the blame on higher storage and memory costs, the company warned consumers to expect another doubling in consumer prices by the fall of 2027. As long as the now-dubbed RAMageddon continues, expect to pay higher prices for your favorite tech and consumer electronics devices. The bad news is that this crisis is expected to last at least until 2028 and likely beyond.
